questions.prompt: Explain how cell reuse works in `UITableView` and `UICollectionView`. Why is it essential for performance?
questions.modelAnswer: Cell reuse maintains a small pool of allocated cells that covers only the visible screen plus a small buffer. As cells scroll off-screen, UIKit moves them into a reuse queue. When new rows scroll in, `dequeueReusableCell` reclaims an existing cell from the queue instead of instantiating a new view. This prevents memory spikes and maintains smooth scrolling without dropping frames.

rubric.criterion: Explains off-screen cells enter a reuse queue and are reclaimed by dequeueReusableCell.
Explains recycling prevents memory spikes and frame drops across large datasets.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of `prepareForReuse()` in custom cells and what problems occur if you omit proper cleanup?
questions.modelAnswer: `prepareForReuse()` runs right before a recycled cell is returned from the dequeue queue. Developers use it to reset cell state: clearing text, resetting images, and canceling pending image download tasks. If cleanup is omitted, late network responses can complete after scrolling and overwrite newly displayed cells with wrong photos, producing visual flickering artifacts.

rubric.criterion: Explains prepareForReuse resets visual state and cancels active asynchronous download tasks.
Describes visual glitches and stale image overwrites when fast scrolling recycled cells.

questions.prompt: Compare Diffable Data Sources with traditional index-path-based `UITableViewDataSource`. What problems do diffable sources solve?
questions.modelAnswer: Traditional data sources rely on manual index path counting via `numberOfRows` and `cellForRowAt`. When updating data, manual batch updates often fell out of sync with data models, causing `NSInternalInconsistencyException` crashes. Diffable Data Sources replace manual index paths with snapshots of `Hashable` items. UIKit calculates differences in the background and applies insertions, deletions, and moves with automatic animations.

rubric.criterion: Identifies manual index path math and batch update synchronization crashes in legacy sources.
Explains snapshots of Hashable items calculate diffs and animations automatically.

questions.prompt: Explain the four-tier hierarchy of `UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout` (Item, Group, Section, Layout).
questions.modelAnswer: Compositional Layout organizes collection layouts into four levels: 1. `NSCollectionLayoutItem` defines individual cell sizing. 2. `NSCollectionLayoutGroup` arranges items in horizontal or vertical rows. 3. `NSCollectionLayoutSection` groups collections of groups, configuring insets, headers, and scrolling behaviors. 4. `UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout` is the root layout object combining all sections on the collection view.

rubric.criterion: Explains Item defines individual cell size and Group arranges items horizontally or vertically.
Explains Section groups items with headers/insets and Layout combines sections for the view.

questions.prompt: What is orthogonal scrolling in Compositional Layout and why is it superior to nesting collection views?
questions.modelAnswer: Orthogonal scrolling enables a collection view section to scroll perpendicularly to the main layout, such as a horizontal carousel inside a vertical list. In legacy UIKit, developers embedded a collection view inside a table cell, causing gesture conflicts, memory waste, and complex delegates. Orthogonal scrolling eliminates nesting; the parent collection view manages cell reuse and scrolling natively.

rubric.criterion: Defines orthogonal scrolling as perpendicular horizontal scrolling within vertical lists.
Explains it eliminates gesture collisions, nested delegates, and duplicate reuse pools.
